bonds_big.h:
THE BIG PICTURE · AS OF NOV 6 CLOSE
A strong October jobs report put a December hike back in focus: payrolls rose 165,000 against forecasts near 60,000, unemployment slipped to 4.1%, and December hike odds jumped to 77% from 69%. Short yields led: the 2-year rose 5 bp to 4.51% and the 10-year 2 bp to 4.86%. Even so, the 10-year ended the week 8 bp below last Friday, after Thursday's AI-stock rout pulled money into Treasuries.
4.86% 10-yr, Nov 6 close−8 bp since last Friday77% December hike odds
📍 What's happening
  • Jobs beat by a wide margin. October payrolls rose 165,000, and August and September were revised up a combined 84,000; wages rose 0.4% on the month and 3.1% over the year.
  • Hike odds rebounded. Kalshi and Polymarket priced a December hike at about 77% (Nov 6, 11:30 AM ET), up from 69% on Nov 5. Later hikes look less likely: January is about 21% and March 42%, down from 24% and 55%.
  • The curve flattened. The 2-year rose more than the 10-year and 30-year (5.26%), so the gap between the 2- and 10-year narrowed to 35 bp from 38 bp.
  • Stocks steadied. The Nasdaq rose 1.1% and the S&P 500 0.3% after Thursday's 5.5% and 4.4% drops, but both lost about 3% for the week; the VIX eased to 25.64 and Brent ended at $98.32, down from $113.43 last Friday.
🏢 What it means for real estate
  • Floating-rate debt is the pressure point. A December hike, now about 77% priced, would lift SOFR-based bridge and construction loans by a quarter point.
  • Fixed-rate quotes barely moved. The 10-year at 4.86% is 45 bp below its Oct 5 high of 5.31%, and Mortgage News Daily's 30-year held at 7.17% after the report; Freddie Mac's was 7.18% on Nov 5.
  • Credit spreads widened. The high-yield spread rose 16 bp to 348 bp on Nov 5 during the stock rout, and investment grade to 93 bp, which offsets part of the Treasury rally for CMBS and bridge borrowers.
  • Leverage is still thin. Multifamily and industrial cap rates (~5.20%) sit about 34 bp over the 10-year, versus 230–340 bp historically, and multifamily CMBS delinquency is 8.04%.
🧭 Where we think it's headed
Most likely4.70–5.05%

The 10-year stays near current levels through year-end as the Fed hikes in December but signals few follow-ups, and a firm job market offsets the pull from weaker stocks.

Risk-off returns4.40–4.70%

The AI selloff resumes, a soft October CPI on Nov 10 pulls December hike odds well below 77%, or a U.S.–Iran deal sends oil lower.

Hawkish turn5.05–5.35%

A hot CPI on Nov 10, weak demand at next week's $125B refunding, or an oil rebound above $110 pushes yields back toward the 5.31% high of Oct 5.

▲ Risks that push yields higher
  1. A December hike. About 77% priced on Nov 6, up from 69% a day earlier; two officials already voted for a hike on Oct 28.
  2. A firm labor market. October payrolls rose 165,000, unemployment is 4.1% and September job openings were 7.52M.
  3. Sticky inflation. PCE is 3.6% and core 3.1%; CPI was 3.7% and PPI 6.3% from a year earlier in September.
  4. Heavy borrowing. Treasury sells $125B of 3-, 10- and 30-year debt next week and expects to borrow $800B in Jan–Mar after $618B in Oct–Dec.
  5. Strong growth. Q3 GDP grew 3.4%, and ISM manufacturing was 55.5 in October.
  6. An oil rebound. Brent is $98.32; a setback in U.S.–Iran talks could push it back toward the $113.43 of Oct 30.
▼ Things that could pull yields lower
  1. A deeper AI unwind. The Nasdaq lost 3.4% this week, including a 5.5% drop on Nov 5, and the VIX is still 25.64.
  2. Cheaper oil. Brent fell to $98.32 from $113.43 last Friday; a lasting U.S.–Iran deal would ease fuel and inflation pressure.
  3. Fewer hikes after December. Odds of a January hike fell to about 21% and March to 42%.
  4. Cooling wages. Hourly earnings are up 3.1% over the year, and private wage growth slowed to 3.1% in Q3, the least since 2021.

bonds_head.h: Who is borrowing, how much, and at what price: Treasury auctions, jumbo corporate and municipal deals, and credit spreads. A strong October jobs report lifted short yields on Friday: the 2-year rose 5 bp to 4.51% and the 10-year 2 bp to 4.86%, though the 10-year is still 8 bp below last Friday after Thursday's AI-stock rout. Big Tech kept borrowing through the selloff, with Meta selling $15B of U.S. bonds and a €9B euro debut and Apple $7.5B. Credit spreads widened during the rout, with high yield up 16 bp to 348 bp and investment grade at 93 bp on Nov 5. Next week's refunding is $58B of 3-year notes, $42B of 10-year notes and $25B of 30-year bonds.

bonds_tsy.h: Next week brings the $125B November refunding: $58B of 3-year notes Mon, Nov 9, $42B of 10-year notes Tue, Nov 10 and $25B of 30-year bonds Thu, Nov 12, which refund about $97B of maturing debt and raise about $28B of new cash. Treasury held sizes on Nov 4 but now expects to keep coupon and FRN sizes unchanged "for the next several quarters," without the earlier "at least." It plans up to $70B of liquidity buybacks next quarter, and borrowing estimates are $618B for Oct–Dec and $800B for Jan–Mar. No coupon auctions were held this week; marketable debt reached $32.1T at the end of October, with bills up $264B on the month to $7.38T.

bonds_tsy_note.h: The sales arrive after a strong jobs report lifted short yields: the 3-year, which auctions Monday, closed at 4.59% on Nov 6, up 6 bp on the day. The 10-year sale on Nov 10 comes the same morning as October CPI, with the 10-year at 4.86%, 45 bp below its early-October high, and the 30-year on Nov 12 follows the Nov 11 bond-market holiday; October's 30-year cleared at 5.618%, against a 5.26% close on Nov 6. With a December hike about 77% priced, a hot CPI would test demand, while renewed stock selling would support it.

cap_caps.h: Core cap rates by sector against a 10-year that closed at 4.86% on Friday, Nov 6. Multifamily and industrial, both at 5.20%, price about 34 bp above the 10-year, versus 2010–2020 average spreads of 230 bp and 340 bp; strip retail at 6.40% and office at 7.40% sit about 154 bp and 254 bp above, against historical averages of 320 bp and 280 bp, and hotel at 8.50% is about 364 bp above, with no historical average given. Recent pricing shows the gap between sectors: the Hyatt Centric Faneuil Hall sold for $58.4M (about $358K per room), 100 Summer St. went at a foreclosure auction for $260M (about $236/SF, 68% below its 2019 price), and a Stop & Shop and Staples-anchored center in Westborough is set for a Dec 8 foreclosure auction.

cap_cmbs.h: CMBS delinquency by property type in September (Trepp). Office is still the stress point at 12.16%, up from 12.00% in August, and multifamily rose to 8.04% from 7.69%, passing retail, which fell to 6.58% from 7.20%. Lodging rose to 6.18% and industrial held at 1.14%; Trepp's October figures were not yet available here as of Nov 6. Local distress keeps surfacing: a 371,425 SF grocery-anchored center in Westborough with a $30.75M mortgage is set for a Dec 8 foreclosure auction, and 100 Summer St. sold for $260M versus $806M in 2019. Credit spreads widened during Thursday's stock rout, with high yield up 16 bp to 348 bp and investment grade at 93 bp on Nov 5.

cap_cost.h: Building costs are still climbing: the Turner Building Cost Index rose 1.48% in Q3 to 1,575, up 5.49% from a year earlier, and construction input prices were up 11.7% year over year in September, led by diesel (+115.2%), energy (+69.9%) and metals. Construction employment changed little in October, and construction hourly earnings were up 4.3% over the year in September. Energy has eased: Brent ended the week at $98.32, down from $113.43 on Oct 30, and ISM's manufacturing prices-paid gauge eased to 75.2 in October from 77.9, though it remains high. October PPI on Nov 13 will mostly predate the oil drop, so replacement costs stay elevated for now.

cap_fed.h: A strong jobs report pushed prediction markets back toward a December hike: about 77% on Nov 6 (Kalshi 77.5%, Polymarket 76.5%, 11:30 AM ET), up from about 69% on Nov 5, after October payrolls rose 165,000 against forecasts near 60,000 and unemployment slipped to 4.1%. The 2-year rose 5 bp to 4.51% and the 10-year 2 bp to 4.86%. Markets see fewer hikes after December: Kalshi puts January at about 21%, down from 24%, and March at 42%, down from 55%. The Fed held at 3.75–4.00% on Oct 28 with two dissents for a hike.

cap_fed_note.h: Odds are a snapshot from Nov 6, 11:30 AM ET via DeFi Rate, after the 8:30 AM jobs report. Kalshi priced a December hike at 77.5% (its meeting table shows 79%) and Polymarket at 76.5%; treat the figures as approximate. Kalshi's meeting table shows January at 21% hike and 75% hold, March 42% and April 13%; some rows add to more than 100%. Next: the $58B 3-year auction on Nov 9, October CPI at 8:30 AM on Nov 10, the same day as the $42B 10-year auction, and October PPI on Nov 13.

cap_fuel.h: Oil ended the week sharply lower: Brent settled at $98.32 on Friday, little changed on the day but down from $113.43 on Oct 30, as hopes grew that the midterm results could ease the U.S.–Israeli conflict with Iran; WTI was $90.83. Pump prices lag: EIA's latest weekly prices available here, still for Oct 26, show U.S. diesel at $6.352 (+$2.634 from a year ago), New England diesel at $6.421 and Boston gasoline at $4.176. Diesel feeds construction, trucking and heating costs (diesel producer prices were up 115.2% in September), so oil near $100 still keeps winter operating budgets well above last year's.

cap_opex.h: Property insurance is getting cheaper: commercial property premiums fell 6.3% in Q2, the fourth straight quarterly decline, though umbrella liability rose 5.3%. Energy remains the pressure point: winter heating oil costs are projected up 31% per household and Eversource NH's winter rate is 17.32¢ per kWh (up 10%). Oil eased this week, with Brent at $98.32 on Nov 6 versus $113.43 on Oct 30, but EIA's New England diesel was still $6.421 in the latest week available (Oct 26). Labor costs are firm: hourly earnings rose 3.1% over the year in October, and employer health insurance costs rose 6.4% over the year in Q3.

cap_rates.h: Treasury curve over the past year. The 10-year closed at 4.86% on Friday, Nov 6, up 2 bp on the day after a strong October jobs report but 8 bp lower since last Friday, after Thursday's AI-stock rout pushed it to 4.84%, its lowest close since Sep 9. The 2-year rose 5 bp to 4.51% as December hike odds climbed to 77%, and the 30-year 1 bp to 5.26%, narrowing the 2- to 10-year gap to 35 bp. The 10-year is 45 bp below its 52-week high of 5.31% on Oct 5 but 68 bp higher this year. The Fed holds at 3.75–4.00%.

cap_supply.h: Pipelines are shrinking in most Sun Belt metros, with 2026 deliveries projected down 47% in Austin, 40% in Phoenix and more than half in Denver, while Nashville completions are down 41%. Miami's pipeline is still expanding (above 8% of inventory) and Charlotte's is among the highest in the U.S. (above 8%). Boston has 14,523 units in its pipeline, with absorption running ahead of deliveries this year and vacancy at 5.6%. Local supply is still arriving slowly: voters rejected Question 7 on smaller suburban lots by about 1.2 points (AP call, Nov 6), keeping lot-size rules local; a Brighton developer wants to triple an approved project to 143 apartments; Revere is weighing a 40R district for a 1,700-unit public housing rebuild that would not start for four to five years; and Malden cut its affordable-unit requirement to 10% from 15%. Boston rents are still rising but cooling into winter: Zumper's October 1-bedroom median was $2,980 (+2.8% YoY, −0.7% on the month), Zillow's September metro rent $2,987 (+2.3%) and Apartment List's October metro median $2,233 (+1.0%).

con_head.h: Households are running on a thinner cushion: the saving rate fell to 3.8% in September 2026, the lowest since 2022, and Michigan sentiment ended October at 48.0, near record lows, while median wage growth held at 3.9% in September and bank card delinquency eased to 2.85% in Q2. Spending is still holding up, with real retail sales up 2.5% from a year earlier in September, which favors grocery, value and off-price tenants and argues for watching collections from lower-income renters.

mig_fc.h: Nationally, 227,548 foreclosure filings were recorded in H1 2026, 0.16% of housing units and up 21.26% from a year earlier. Bank repossessions (REO) reached 27,983, up 33%, and foreclosure starts were 164,566, up 18%. The latest monthly figure available here, for August, was 40,277 filings, up 1% from the prior month and 13% from a year earlier. Florida (0.27%), South Carolina (0.26%), Delaware and Indiana (0.25%) and Illinois (0.23%) had the highest state rates in H1. Massachusetts had 2,719 filings, a rate of 0.09% (one in 1,115 units), up 3.23% from a year earlier; New Hampshire had 488, a rate of 0.08% (one in 1,329 units), up 23.54%. Both rates are well below the national rate. ATTOM's Q3 foreclosure report could not be found here as of Nov 6.
